citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
There is one ~6 year old female pronghorn named "Thunder" and one ~16 year old female mule deer named "Velcro" with
very overgrown front hooves. Although neither animal is overtly lame upon observation, the overgrowth is forcing the
heels downward when the animals bear weight on the affected limbs. The facility representative told the inspector they
had not realized how long the hooves had become and that they usually just wait for the hooves to break off on their own.
When this was discussed during the inspection, the representative sent a text message to the attending veterinarian to
request guidance and make a plan for managing the hooves on these two animals.
When hooves become so long that they alter the natural angles of the feet and lower legs, this causes strain and
weakening of soft tissue support structures. Failure to communicate the problem to the attending veterinarian delays
intervention and increases the likelihood that pain, lameness and permanent damage will occur. The licensee must
ensure that adequate daily observation of all animals is done to assess their health and well-being, and that there is a
mechanism of direct and frequent communication so that timely and accurate information on problems of animal health,
behavior and well being is conveyed to the attending veterinarian.
CORRECT BY DEVELOPING A PLAN WITH THE ATTENDING VETERINARIAN FOR MANAGEMENT OF THE
OVERGROWN HOOVES BY 07/27/2026

The enclosure housing an adult female elk named "Chama" has a section of fence that is in disrepair, patched with
broken and stretched chicken wire and partially covered with small, unattached, weathered boards that are easily pushed
aside. The hole measures ~1 foot by 2 foot. The facility representative had a worker repair the fence when discovered
during the inspection.
Damaged fences can permit entry of predators and are an entrapment and injury hazard for the animals inside the
enclosure. The facility must be constructed of such material and of such strength as appropriate for the animals involved.
The indoor and outdoor housing facilities shall be structurally sound and shall be maintained in good repair to protect the
animals from injury and to contain the animals.
CORRECTED AT THE TIME OF INSPECTION
This is a 1st Re-License Inspection for a Class “C” license. The inspection and exit briefing were conducted with the
applicant.
All items must be in compliance within 2 more inspections or by 09/21/2026 or the applicant will forfeit the license fee and
must wait 6 months to reapply. Please contact your inspector to schedule your next Re-License Inspection.
Regulated activity can continue under your existing USDA license until it expires.
